title: Katherine Deves among four NSW upper house candidates revealed by One Nation
summary:
Party’s NSW leader Mike Newman says contenders are ‘people from the real world’ and not ‘career politicians’

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The failed federal Liberal candidate Katherine Deves, who campaigned to exclude transgender women from women’s sport, will stand for One Nation at next year’s New South Wales election.

Deves was among four NSW Legislative Council candidates announced by One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, on Sunday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The failed federal Liberal candidate Katherine Deves, who campaigned to exclude transgender women from women’s sport, will stand for One Nation at next year’s New South Wales election.

Deves was among four NSW Legislative Council candidates announced by One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, on Sunday.

The other candidates were Arnon Wither, a construction worker from the Hunter region who works as an electorate officer for Senator Sean Bell; Manti Steele, a farmer, teacher and mother of eight from Dubbo; and Daniel Hill, a surf lifesaver from the state’s south coast.

The NSW election will be held on 13 March.

Newman said on Sunday the upper house candidates were “authentic”, “people from the real world” and not “career politicians”.

One Nation has only announced a single lower house candidate – Newman, in the electorate of Cessnock – but he said the party would run candidates in all 93 lower house seats.

“We want to make sure that these people bleed orange, and like I said, they’re all from the real world,” he said.

“That’s the that’s the type of person we’re aiming at … people from the real world who understand business, who understand their pinch points and pain points, understand the cost of living, understand cashflow.”

Deves was handpicked by the former prime minister Scott Morrison to run in the federal NSW seat of Warringah in 2022. Her candidacy was marred by controversy, including when she likened anti-trans activism to standing up against the Holocaust.

On Sunday she said she joined One Nation “because I wanted to be a part of the rescue, recovery, and restoration of our nation”.

“We are seeing cost of living skyrocket, whether it’s fuel, housing, energy, and we are watching a government that is so wedded to destructive ideologies like DEI and net zero that they are prepared to impoverish us all,” she said.

If elected, she would look to make changes to state laws regarding “discrimination, hate speech, vilification, birth certificates, etc”.

“Where we can restore clear and accurate language around biological sex, men and women, and ensure that women and girls are safe and have spaces for services, sports, etc, where it’s inappropriate for males to be there.”

One Nation has required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media.

News24 reported last month that Deves would run as an upper house candidate in the NSW election. She announced that she joined One Nation in September.

title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
summary:
From a bamboo gym in Bali to a house made from earth in Wiltshire, these projects show the beauty in sustainable design

With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil

Continue reading...
full_text:
With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil

In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.

The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.

David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”

The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.

The Arc, Bali, Indonesia

The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.

Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.

Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”

Sara Kulturhus, Skellefteå, Sweden

Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.

The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.

“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”

The Forest, Hobart, Australia

When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.

At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.

“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”

Rammed Earth House, Cranborne Chase, UK

On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.

The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.

Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”

“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

title: ‘We need to get back to class’: some teachers lose patience as France enters its eighth week of student protests
summary:
Educators voice concerns as thousands of children facing exams miss up to 150 hours of class

For several weeks, Alex, 16, has woken at 4am and walked 90 minutes in the dark from his northern Paris suburb so he can help gather wheelie bins to blockade his high school in Vincennes.

In a tote bag, he brings some masks and some swimming goggles in case of police teargas. His parents, who work in the arts and vote left, support the French school student protesters who since September have blocked schools demanding repairs to dilapidated school buildings, more replacement teachers, a solution to overcrowded classes and more equality in the university application system.

full_text:
For several weeks, Alex, 16, has woken at 4am and walked 90 minutes in the dark from his northern Paris suburb so he can help gather wheelie bins to blockade his high school in Vincennes.

In a tote bag, he brings some masks and some swimming goggles in case of police teargas. His parents, who work in the arts and vote left, support the French school student protesters who since September have blocked schools demanding repairs to dilapidated school buildings, more replacement teachers, a solution to overcrowded classes and more equality in the university application system.

“But this week, my mum woke up early and said to me: ‘Do you really think you need to blockade again today?’’ said Alex. “She supports me but is starting to think I’m doing too much. But how else can we make ourselves heard? We can’t stop now. It’s the only way the government will listen.”

His 17-year-old friend, also on the school barricade with dozens of pupils this week, said: “Any progress that has been won in France has been achieved through people demonstrating on the street.”

France is entering the eighth week of an unprecedented schools crisis. The biggest youth protest movement in decades has over the past two months seen hundreds of high schools barricaded with wheelie bins or shut amid security fears.

The government is now facing criticism of its handling of the crisis. It first responded with a security crackdown, mobilising riot police outside schools across France amid clashes that led to injuries from police weaponry, including children who lost a hand or an eye.

Then over the past two weeks, the government attempted to argue that its offer to decrease some class sizes and review the university application platform meant the movement was coming to an end.

But in recent days, the government has been accused by teachers’ unions of letting the protests fester into an increasingly dangerous mood of violence. Fireworks have been fired outside schools and inside classrooms in different parts of France.

A local councillor outside Paris was hit in the chest by a bottle of gasoline as she was trying to mediate outside a school. One education trade unionist said a school principal had bought a bulletproof vest for protection.

The government and teachers’ unions have said that individuals committing violence outside or inside schools were not the same people as students who were peacefully protesting for education rights.

But high school principals held their own demonstrations on Friday, saying they were struggling to cope with the confusion and chaos. At least 50 principals have made requests to quit their posts. More than 360 schoolchildren and 245 staff have been injured since the protests started.

So many weeks of classes have now been missed that one teacher, who demonstrated outside a central Paris police station this week after one of her pupils was arrested, said: “There is absolute uncertainty over how we can return to proper teaching. This is becoming an intractable situation with no end in sight.”

Thousands of French children in key baccalauréat (the French A-levels) exam years – even children who are not protesting directly – have now missed up to 150 hours of teaching at schools that have been barricaded daily or closed regularly for security reasons since the end of September. This is particularly acute in the Paris area, and in other cities such as Toulouse.

Online lessons have rarely fully replaced missed classes. Many teenagers are at home in their fourth or fifth week of no school. Some parents are beginning to wake early to stand outside schools themselves to try to individually stop wheelie bin barricades – sometimes leading to more clashes.

Police are increasingly stationed outside schools, sometimes hitting students’ hands with truncheons to make them loosen their grip on bins, as happened in central Paris this week.

“The French administration is trying to impose a kind of smokescreen of wishful thinking, that everything is alright, stiff-upper-lip, no problem, but everyone needs to face up to what is happening,” said Julien Roy, 52, who teaches history and geography at Lycée Balzac in the central city of Tours and represents the SNALC education union in Indre-et-Loire. “There is a crisis of trust. We need a de-escalation of violence and a path back to education.”

Roy’s school has been at the centre of the protests since the end of September when, on the pavement outside, a 16-year-old school student from a different school, lost the use of his eye after he was allegedly struck by a police rubber bullet.

“There is still constant tension,” said Roy. He added that in recent weeks firework mortars had been set off, sometimes aimed at staff, and fires had been started in bins and materials for molotov cocktails were found in a building opposite the school.

Police were regularly present. Staff felt individuals not connected to the school were involved in the violence. He said stress was taking a toll on staff: 10 colleagues were on sick leave, including his principal and deputy principal.

“We need to get back to class to teach our pupils again, some of whom are booing us,” Roy said. “We’ll have to sit down and talk about this, honestly and calmly, to get it out of everyone’s system so we can restore trust.”

He said: “There are children who are suffering, and many of them we’re not seeing because they are stuck at home. Some pupils approach school, see the police, panic and go away, because they can’t bear this atmosphere with police outside school. There are fragile teenagers with difficulties at school who can’t come in, and those children are shattered by this.”

He said: “What is lethal is that we’re leading children to conclude that it’s only through violence that they can be heard, that violence is legitimate and nothing can be gained through negotiation … this is going to leave an impact on society, creating future adults who are going to feel bitter and broken.”

At a high school in the Créteil area, an English teacher said: “I feel proud of my students’ peaceful protests. The children demonstrating are asking for the same thing teachers have wanted for years: more resources, more dignity in teaching environments. Teachers’ strikes haven’t been listened to, whereas students see they are having an impact.

“But with a presidential election next spring, and the start of electoral season, it’s difficult to imagine that this is going to stop. I do worry about students’ exams. One former colleague said to me that this school year could be a write-off.”

Students’ names have been changed

title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
summary:
In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem

In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.

When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan.

Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme

full_text:
In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.

When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan.

The majority studying in the department were young women, and a few of us were of African descent. Some classmates and I raised concerns within the department at the time, but nothing was ever done: his “freedom” of speech was something we had to just accept. Years after we left Leeds, a group of us felt so strongly about what we had experienced – and the university’s failure in its duty of care – that we wrote a letter about it.

I have been transported back to those Leeds seminar rooms after reading of the decision of Oriel College at the University of Oxford to allow Dr Nathan Cofnas to speak at an event organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society, a student group that supports Reform UK. Much like Ellis, Cofnas has persistently espoused views associated with scientific racism.

A blogpost published by Cofnas while he worked at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, claimed that “in a meritocracy, Harvard faculty would be recruited from the best of the best students, which means the number of black professors would approach 0%” and that Black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. Though Cofnas’s right to his views were upheld by a tribunal, it found that the blogpost “created a hostile, intimidating, unwelcoming and degrading environment for members of the college, particularly black students”. Cofnas’s claims against Prof Jason Arday also led to the professor facing intense media scrutiny in the runup to his death.

For me, this story is a painful and sobering reminder that little has changed when it comes to universities’ care for their students, particularly Black students. In a statement regarding the Cofnas event, Oriel College said that the institution is “committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive.”

Perhaps the argument that platforming racist ideas is merely a “freedom of expression” issue persists because of a disconnect with the real experience of Black students – and faculty – who have to navigate university campuses under such circumstances. Nearly three decades on, I can still remember preparing myself for tutorials with Ellis. Trying to defend my right to exist, to be in that space. And I wasn’t the only one. Rehearsing arguments, sharpening comebacks, compiling data. Anything I could do to try to push back at whatever derogatory comment he would slip into his lecture.

I was brought up to be conscious, proud of my heritage and culture. Maybe I landed a blow or two, but the upshot was that it was exhausting. It was never enough. I was never going to change his mind, but I was not mature enough to realise that. And it chip, chip, chipped away at me, my self-esteem, my emotional wellbeing. At a time when I should have felt liberated, encouraged – and, yes, challenged – to explore, interrogate, critically analyse, I was being pushed into a box. The message was clear: know your place, Ebony.

Advocates of free speech may think that what I endured was OK, and similarly that Black and global-majority students at Oxford must simply suck it up with regard to Cofnas. But as a young Black woman on the receiving end of anti-Black as well as misogynistic speech from a person who had power over me, it felt like abuse.

And as for Oxford, while freedom of speech is indeed a fundamental human right, it also sits alongside an obligation, according to the UN, to “ensure the equal and non-discriminatory participation of all individuals in public life”. This means that universities must balance academic freedom with their duties under UK equality legislation.

It may be that Oriel College has considered both these obligations and done the necessary equality analysis, in which case it should share it transparently with students, academics and high-profile figures who have raised legitimate concerns. But otherwise, this just looks like yet another case of disregarding the safety of Black people who simply want to study, work and live their lives without their intelligence being questioned.

Inoltre, la pista Vagliana, in zona Grostè, continuerà a essere chiusa a mezzogiorno per una nuova battitura: «dalle 13.00 in poi, una superficie perfetta come al mattino». Poi una novità da Pinzolo-Doss del Sabion con la nuova pista Plaza, prolungamento della pista Brenta. Il nuovo tracciato scende da località Puza dai Fò fino a Ponte Plaza, dove si trova la stazione intermedia della Pinzolo-Campiglio Express. Quanto ai prezzi, sottolinea Felicetti, si applica la tariffa dinamica che varia a seconda del periodo di acquisto. «I costi hanno subito un aumento del 3% per cento - sottolinea - e il prezzo dinamico va dai 59 agli 89 euro. title: Bureau veritas, allarme infrastrutture: «Più fragili col cambiamento climatico»
summary: L’ente di certificazione Bureau veritas lancia l’allarme sulla salute delle infrastrutture (quali viadotti, ferrovie e gallerie) in Italia: uno studio di Nexta, società d’ingegneria del gruppo, sostiene che non è...
full_text:
L’ente di certificazione Bureau veritas lancia l’allarme sulla salute delle infrastrutture (quali viadotti, ferrovie e gallerie) in Italia: uno studio di Nexta, società d’ingegneria del gruppo, sostiene che non è soltanto la vetustà a essere pericolosa ma anche, e in modo sempre più incisivo, i cambiamenti climatici. Il contesto generale, sottolinea Carla Formenti, direttore tecnico b&i (business & industry) di Nexta, «sta cambiando rapidamente a causa dell’evoluzione climatica e dell’aumento della frequenza o dell’intensità di alcuni eventi meteorologici estremi. E ciò rappresenta un rischio e un problema da affrontare, specie per le opere più datate, progettate sulla base di dati climatici e idrologici che potrebbero non rappresentare più adeguatamente le condizioni attuali. La questione, che si pone con particolare intensità in zone sovraesposte come Alpi e Appennini, non riguarda soltanto la resistenza della struttura, ma anche la sua capacità di continuare a svolgere la propria funzione in sicurezza».

In Italia, prosegue Formenti, «la rete infrastrutturale comprende circa 600mila chilometri di strade, oltre 16mila chilometri di linee ferroviarie, circa 240mila ponti e viadotti censiti e 3.500 gallerie. Circa il 60-70% di queste opere è stata realizzata più di 30 anni fa, sulla base di condizioni climatiche, idrologiche e territoriali diverse da quelle attuali. Basti pensare che, secondo l’Ispra, nel 2023 il 18,4% del territorio nazionale risultava a rischio frana e il 4,1% a rischio alluvione, nello scenario di pericolosità più elevata; e ora, su questo scenario, impatta anche la tendenza di variabilità dei valori climatici in Italia, che confermano un incremento veloce delle temperature, una riduzione della piovosità con importante incremento di intensità dei singoli eventi».

Tutto questo impone, si legge nello studio, «un approccio forzatamente innovativo in tema di controlli e ispezioni. Queste non possono limitarsi alla ricerca di difettologia: fessure, deformazioni, corrosione o altri danni visibili. È necessario verificare anche se siano cambiate le condizioni per le quali le opere erano state progettate. Un’infrastruttura può, infatti, mantenere un aspetto apparentemente integro, ma trovarsi a operare in un ambiente più gravoso rispetto a quello considerato in origine».

Ogni infastruttura, in effetti, rileva il report Nexta, «viene progettata sulla base di determinate condizioni ambientali, idrologiche, geologiche e geotecniche.
